newsitem.title: HONG KONG: China general says PLA won't mess with Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: China general says PLA won't mess with Hong Kong.

text.p: The general who guards the political purity of China's future Hong Kong garrison said on Friday the People's Liberation Army (PLA) would not meddle in local government or business after Beijing takes over on July 1.

Major-General Xiong Zi Ren, political commissar of the PLA garrison, also said at a seminar on Hong Kong's transition from British to Chinese rule that the army would have its own lawyers in Hong Kong to make sure it did not break the law.
Any soldier violating Hong Kong's laws while off-duty would be handed over to Hong Kong civilian authorities for judgement.

He noted that under British colonial rule, London's governor in Hong Kong, currently Chris Patten, was commander-in-chief of the British garrison, but after the flag change the territory's government and the military would become separate entities.
"The Hong Kong garrison and government will be independent military and administrative systems with no affiliate relationship and will not interfere with each other," he said.
Xiong gave assurances the PLA would stick to its duty of defending Hong Kong and would not dabble in commerce.
"Some Hong Kong compatriots worry whether the garrison will respect regulations, or whether they will run businesses.
"I can categorically tell you that we resolutely will abide by all regulations set out in the law," Xiong said.
"We have already set a rule that bans involvement in production business," he said.

He said the PLA unit would bring a team of lawyers from China to deal with legal problems, cooperate with local legal bodies, and ensure the troops adhered to Hong Kong's Beijing-imposed constitution, the Basic Law, as well as to local laws.

The Basic Law guarantees that Hong Kong can function as a separate entity from the rest of China with its own distinct political and economic system, little changed from the present freewheeling set-up, for a further 50 years after the handover.

Many of Hong Kong's 6.4 million people fear the PLA, recalling its violent crackdown against pro-democracy students in Beijing in 1989. China is expected to include up to 10,000 troops in the garrison, although some may remain stationed over the border in China proper.

China gave Hong Kong people a first glimpse of some of the PLA garrison's military hardware on Thursday when it opened a big aviation show in the territory, flaunting fighter jets, helicopters and other technology.
Britain and China are currently haggling over the size and activities of a PLA advance party that China wants to send in before July 1, and on the date of its arrival.
